lesson.title: Perfectly Balanced Charge, By Design
lesson.summary: A nonpolar molecule is one in which bond dipoles cancel by symmetry, or in which the bonds themselves carry no significant charge separation, leaving no net dipole moment.
lesson.body:
A nonpolar molecule is the other possible outcome of the vector summing process described in molecular polarity: the bond dipoles add up to zero, or there is no meaningful bond dipole to begin with. There are really two distinct routes to nonpolarity, and it helps to keep them separate. The first route is having bonds that are not very polar in the first place, which happens when the atoms involved have similar electronegativities. The second, and more common route among molecules built from polar bonds, is geometric cancellation, where individual bond dipoles are polar but symmetry forces their vector sum to zero.

Diatomic elements like N2, O2, and Cl2 illustrate the first route. Since both atoms in the bond are identical, there is no electronegativity difference at all, so the bond has no dipole and the molecule is automatically nonpolar. Methane, CH4, illustrates the second route in a slightly more interesting way. Each C-H bond does have a small dipole, since carbon is a bit more electronegative than hydrogen, but methane's tetrahedral geometry places four identical bonds pointing toward the corners of a tetrahedron with 109.5 degree angles between them. This arrangement is symmetric enough that the four bond dipole vectors sum to exactly zero, leaving methane nonpolar overall despite containing polar bonds.

Carbon dioxide is worth revisiting here from the nonpolar side. Its linear shape places the two polar C=O bonds at exactly 180 degrees, so they point in precisely opposite directions and cancel completely. This is a useful contrast case for students because it is easy to mistakenly assume that any molecule containing polar bonds must itself be polar; CO2 is the standard counterexample showing that geometry, not just bond identity, determines the outcome. Boron trifluoride, BF3, gives a third example: it is trigonal planar with three identical, polar B-F bonds spaced 120 degrees apart in a flat triangle, and that threefold symmetry is also enough to cancel the net dipole to zero.

Recognizing nonpolar molecules matters because their lack of a permanent dipole changes how they interact with their surroundings. Nonpolar molecules do not attract each other, or attract polar molecules, through permanent charge separation, so their intermolecular attractions come from a different and generally weaker source, London dispersion forces, which are covered later in this chapter. This is also why nonpolar substances like oils and greases do not mix with polar water: there is no favorable charge to charge attraction to hold them together, which is the molecular basis of the old rule that like dissolves like. Identifying a molecule as nonpolar therefore requires the same two step check as identifying a polar one: examine the bonds for electronegativity difference, then examine the geometry for symmetry, and confirm the vector sum actually reaches zero rather than assuming it from the formula alone.
